title: What was removed as a hub, and why
question: Which organizations, people and addresses were taken out of the graph because they link everything and mean nothing?
finding: 359 hubs were removed before grouping: 203 by name (public bodies, banks, utilities, title, payroll and insurance firms, law and accounting firms, universities and hospitals), 69 because one kind of link tied them to more than 12 others, and 87 addresses that are office buildings or mail drops. Without the removals the largest connected set would have swallowed most of the graph; with them it still holds 689 of the 1032 linked nodes, which is why large sets are split into cores.
how: Three stated rules. (1) Name: the name contains a word or firm name on the list in the script (for example bank, title, insurance, LLP, university, hospital, or a named utility, payroll processor or audit firm); the whole node is left out. (2) Degree: after loose ends are dropped, any node tied to more than 12 others by a single kind of link loses its links of that kind and keeps the rest; where another screen counts the node's true reach (grantees of a funder, clients of a lobbying firm) that count is used. (3) Address: 25 or more active business registrations at a street address, or a mail-drop or shared-office operator registered there; two parties are still joined if they give the same suite and the suite has fewer than 8 registrations. 'Links' is the number of relationship rows or neighbours that pointed at the hub.
limits: A rule this blunt removes real relationships too: a law firm that is also a permit consultant, a hospital that is also a grantee, an elected official whose committees many linked organizations gave to, a fiscal sponsor with hundreds of grantees. The largest removed by the degree rule was Local Initiatives Support Corp, tied to 10,646 others by the link “pays (grant, contract or rent)” (grant recipients on its own tax returns). Anything in this list can still be looked up in the screen that first recorded it. The name list was written by hand and is not complete; a bank or insurer whose name does not say so is caught only by the degree rule. Any name ending in LLP is treated as a professional partnership, which also catches a few architects and engineers.
